name: Run Gorgonzola Run Burger - Made with Gorgonzola

recipe.history:
Gorgonzola is one of the oldest blue cheeses in the world, with a documented history stretching back to at least the ninth century in the small town of Gorgonzola, situated in the Po Valley just east of Milan in the Lombardy region of northern Italy. According to cheesemaking tradition, Gorgonzola was discovered accidentally — as most great fermented foods are — when a young cheese worker, distracted by a romantic encounter, left partially drained curd out overnight and returned in the morning to find it threaded with green-blue mold. Whether the story is true or merely charming, the technique it describes is accurate: Gorgonzola develops its characteristic Penicillium glaucum veining through a process of inoculation and aeration, with metal rods or needles pierced through the maturing wheels to allow oxygen to penetrate and the mold to bloom. The cheese comes in two principal styles: Gorgonzola Dolce, which is aged for roughly two to three months and has a soft, creamy, spreadable texture and a comparatively mild flavor; and Gorgonzola Piccante, aged for six months to a year or more, which is firmer, more crumbly, sharper, and deeply pungent. Both styles carry Protected Designation of Origin status from the European Union, meaning that authentic Gorgonzola can only be produced in the Lombardy and Piedmont regions of Italy.

Gorgonzola's entry into American cuisine was slower and more contentious than that of Parmesan or mozzarella, largely because blue cheese is a polarizing flavor profile that not everyone is prepared to encounter. American blue cheese — largely domestic versions of Roquefort and Stilton produced in Wisconsin and Indiana — became moderately common in steakhouse salad dressings and wedge salads through the mid-twentieth century, but Italian Gorgonzola specifically began appearing on restaurant menus in earnest during the 1990s and 2000s, as American diners became more adventurous and Italian-American cuisine expanded beyond red sauce. It was the steakhouse that legitimized blue cheese on beef: a filet mignon stuffed with Gorgonzola, or a New York strip with Gorgonzola butter melting across it, became a luxury standard. From steakhouse to burger joint was a short leap. Gorgonzola on a burger delivers an instant complexity that no other cheese quite matches — its saltiness, its funk, and its creamy richness transform a straightforward beef patty into something that feels genuinely sophisticated without requiring any pretension.

I have a complicated relationship with Gorgonzola that began at age eight when my uncle put a piece of Gorgonzola Piccante on my plate at a dinner party and told me it was a special cheese that only adults were allowed to eat. I put it in my mouth immediately and my entire face tried to leave my skull. I spat it into a napkin while the adults laughed. I was angry about this for years, in the way that children are angry about being tricked, and I avoided blue cheese with real conviction until I was in my late twenties and a chef friend melted Gorgonzola Dolce into a pan sauce over a cast iron steak and made me try it on a piece of bread. It was nothing like what I remembered. It was buttery and complex and just barely funky, with a richness that coated the bread and made me want more immediately. I have been buying Gorgonzola ever since. On a burger, Gorgonzola Dolce works best — it softens beautifully over the residual heat of a medium rare patty, spreading across the top of the beef in a creamy, irregular layer. The funk is present but not aggressive. It is the cheese for people who love blue cheese and the cheese that might convert people who thought they didn't.

Medium rare — 130–135°F (54–57°C) — is the temperature at which Gorgonzola and beef reach their fullest mutual expression. Gorgonzola Dolce begins to soften and melt at temperatures just above body heat, which means a medium rare patty at 130°F is already warm enough to start the process. By the time the burger is assembled and reaches the diner, the cheese has spread across the patty's surface in a flowing, uneven layer that mixes with the beef's natural juices. The mold cultures in Gorgonzola produce compounds — particularly diacetyl and methyl ketones — that are fat-soluble and bind directly to the warm beef fat in a medium rare patty, creating a depth of flavor that is impossible to achieve when the fat has been driven out by overcooking. A well-done burger under Gorgonzola is a dry patty under a puddle of oily cheese that has nowhere to go. A medium rare burger under Gorgonzola is a living, integrated thing — the beef and the cheese are speaking to each other, trading fat and funk and salt in a conversation that lasts through every bite. There is no other way to serve this burger with integrity.
ingredients: 1.5 lbs (680g) ground beef, 80/20 chuck, freshly ground
5 oz (140g) Gorgonzola Dolce, at room temperature (crumbled or in a chunk)
2 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened (for toasting buns)
1 large sweet onion (Vidalia or Walla Walla), sliced into 1/4-inch rounds
1/4 cup walnut halves, toasted and roughly chopped
Freshly cracked black pepper for finishing
instructions: 1. Caramelize the onions: melt 2 tablespoons butter in a heavy skillet over medium-low heat. Add the onion rounds, season with salt, and cook for 30–35 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes, until deeply golden and jammy. Add balsamic vinegar and brown sugar in the last 5 minutes and stir to combine. Set aside.
2. Cook bacon strips in a separate skillet over medium heat until rendered and crispy, about 8–10 minutes. Transfer to a paper towel-lined plate.
3. Make the chive sour cream sauce: whisk together mayonnaise, sour cream, fresh chives, lemon juice, and Dijon mustard. Season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until needed.
4. Combine ground beef, kosher salt, black pepper, garlic powder, thyme, and Worcestershire sauce in a large bowl. Mix gently with your hands until just combined.
5. Divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 6 oz / 170g each). Form into patties about 3/4 inch thick, pressing a slight dimple in the center. Refrigerate for at least 20 minutes.
6. Remove Gorgonzola from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking to bring it fully to room temperature — it will melt more evenly over the patty.
7. Heat a cast iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until smoking. Brush lightly with neutral oil.
8. Season the outside of each patty with a pinch of flaky salt. Cook for 3–4 minutes on the first side without moving, until a deep, dark crust has formed.

9. Flip each patty. Crumble or place a generous portion of Gorgonzola Dolce on top of each. Add the tablespoon of butter to the pan and tent loosely with foil. Cook an additional 2–3 minutes until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center reads 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. The Gorgonzola should be softening and beginning to spread.
10. Transfer patties to a wire rack and rest for 3–4 minutes. The Gorgonzola will continue melting and spreading during the rest.
11. Butter the cut sides of the brioche buns and toast cut-side down in the same skillet over medium heat for 1–2 minutes until golden.
12. Assemble each burger: spread chive sour cream sauce on both bun halves. Place a handful of baby arugula on the bottom bun, then a tomato slice.
13. Add the rested patty with melted Gorgonzola. Spoon a mound of balsamic caramelized onions over the cheese. Lay 1–2 strips of crispy bacon across the top.

14. Scatter toasted walnut pieces over the top, drizzle with a thin thread of honey, and finish with a crack of black pepper and a pinch of flaky sea salt. Crown with the top bun and serve immediately.
